abstract: Photobleaching and phototoxicity limit how long living cells can be followed by total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy. We describe an objective-type TIRF microscope illuminated by a picosecond supercontinuum laser spectrally windowed to 20-nm bands, pulse-picked to 1 MHz and delivered through two TIRF illuminators, one per polarisation direction. Single GFP-talin molecules in focal adhesions of living cells were detected throughout uninterrupted recordings of 10-31 min, and drift-corrected, time-stamped localisations resolved adhesion motion of tens of nanometres per minute. In diffraction-limited time-lapse at one frame per second, adhesion brightness, adhesion area, cell footprint and adhesion motility were unchanged after an hour. Under continuous-wave excitation on a comparable commercial TIRF microscope, the same schedule preserved cell behaviour at a low laser setting but adhesions dimmed, and higher settings bleached and retracted cells within a minute of exposure. We provide the datasets and open ImageJ tools for drift correction and localisation.
